title: Why is Krishna blue?
hookLine: the texts call Krishna, Rama and Draupadi dark; so why is he blue on the calendar and fair on the screen?

cards: Look at the calendar on almost any Hindu kitchen wall. Krishna is blue. Not a little blue: sky blue, peacock blue, swimming-pool blue.
Now look at many of the films and TV shows made about him. Often he's played by a fair-skinned actor with a gym body. Then open the old texts.
They agree with neither picture. So which one is he? Today, the color of the gods.

teach.b: Start with his name. In Sanskrit, krishna means dark, even black. Some teachers also hear in it the one who draws you in, from a root that means to pull, and plenty of devotees happily keep both.
But the color is right there in the name.
The devotional poems call him Ghanashyam: dark as a rain cloud, the heavy blue-black cloud just before the monsoon breaks. In songs he's simply Shyam, the dark one. And he isn't alone.
In the Ramayana, Rama too is described as dark.
In the Mahabharata, Draupadi is called Krishnaa, the dark one, for her complexion, and Arjuna says one of his own names, Krishna, came from his dark skin. Dark, and in every case, beautiful.
The one Hindus love as God was pictured dark, and loved for exactly that. So where did the blue come from? Painters reached for the deep blue of a rain cloud, and over the centuries it brightened.
Many devotees add a meaning: blue is the color of the sky and the ocean, the things with no edge. And the fair actors? Posters and films have often cast that way.

teach.h: THE TEXTS NEVER ASKED FOR FAIR.
teach.b: The texts never asked for it. Many Hindus talk about this openly now, and nobody needs to blame one artist to see the gap. Braj even has a Holi story about it.
Little Krishna is upset that he's dark and Radha is fair, and his mother tells him: go and color her face, and then you'll match. Notice what the story never says. It never says he should be lighter.
It says: make everyone the same color for a day.

how: Devotional songs call Krishna Shyam or Ghanashyam, dark as a rain cloud; temple images show him dark, often black stone, and paintings usually show him blue; in Braj, Holi is played in his and Radha's name.

games.q: you're casting a film about Krishna. the producer wants a fair, muscular star. what do the old texts actually describe?
o: they never mention how he looks.
games.why: the poems call him Ghanashyam, dark as a rain cloud, and dwell on his grace. the fair, muscled Krishna came from posters and screens, not the texts.

practice: Bring up the image of Krishna you grew up with, on a wall, a calendar, a screen, and notice its color.
Then let it fade, and picture a monsoon sky: the heavy dark cloud just before the rain, the air cooling, everyone looking up, glad; that's the color the poets chose for the one they loved most.
If your own skin is dark, or the skin of someone you love, let that be the color of the beloved for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Shyama. Dark, the dark one: a name for Krishna, dark as a rain cloud, and praised for it. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: dark, dusky, the color of a rain cloud. in Hindi songs, Shyam is simply Krishna's name.
